title: Just watching
hookLine: Buddhist, Hindu, Christian and Stoic-inspired practice all use the breath, and science studies it: start by only watching

cards: Twenty thousand times a day, roughly, and nobody asks you to. You did it through every story. You're doing it now.
Breathing. Welcome to camp three, the practices: the stories showed what's possible, and now you try things with your own body and your own days. Start with a small experiment.
Notice your breath for a moment, and see how quickly you start controlling it: deeper, slower, trying to do it right. Almost everybody does that. Today is about leaving it alone.

teach.b: Many traditions have noticed the breath, each in its own way. The Buddhist texts have a whole discourse on it, the Anapanasati Sutta, mindfulness of breathing.

The Buddha describes someone sitting in a quiet place, body upright, attention gathered. Breathing in a long breath, they know: I'm breathing in long. Breathing out a short breath, they know: I'm breathing out short.
That's the first step. Not making the breath long. Just knowing it.
In Hindu yoga, the breath is tied to prana, the life-energy, and the Yoga Sutras make breath practice one of the eight limbs of yoga; that's mostly about guiding the breath, which comes later.
In Orthodox Christianity, monks called hesychasts, from a Greek word for stillness, joined the short Jesus Prayer to the rhythm of breathing. And the ancient Stoics?
Honestly, they wrote very little about breathing; modern people who practice Stoic ideas often borrow a pause with the breath from elsewhere, and it's fair to say so.
Researchers, meanwhile, study breathing and attention in labs, and are still learning what it does. So start where the Buddha's instructions start: watching. It's harder than it sounds.
The moment you watch the breath, you want to fix it, make it deeper, make it better. But the breath doesn't need you. It kept you alive all night while you slept.
Just watching means letting it breathe itself, the way you'd watch waves come in without trying to push them. Today you're not the breather. You're the one who notices.

how: Buddhists practice mindfulness of breathing as a core meditation, many yoga practitioners begin with simply observing the breath before breath exercises, and some Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer with the rhythm of their breathing.

games.why: notice, and let go of the wheel. just watching means letting the breath breathe itself. guiding it comes later in the week.

practice: Sit comfortably, upright if you can, hands resting, and find the breath wherever it's easiest to feel: the nose, the chest, the belly.

Don't change it; just watch it come in and go out, count ten breaths like this, then keep watching. If you start steering it, notice, and let go of the wheel; if you lose count, start again at one, which is normal, not failing.

wordCard.voice: Just watching. Noticing the breath without changing it: breathing in long, knowing it's long, and letting it breathe itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: anapanasati, mindfulness (sati) of breathing in and out (anapana).

carryVoice: Your line: it breathes. It doesn't need your help to keep going. See you on day ninety-eight.
